title: Attribution and transformation
brief: The verse locates talk of selves and phenomena in transformations of consciousness; it does not yet explain the three transformations.

words.note: Ātman and dharma are joined inside a compound; upacāra is an applied or transferred designation, not proof of a substantial self.
words.alternative: figurative designation of selves and phenomena

words.note: Hi gives a reason or emphasis; it does not introduce a separate entity.
Vividha qualifies the attribution as taking many forms.
The relative yaḥ introduces what is picked up by asau, “that,” later in the verse.
The middle verb describes coming into operation or occurring.
The locative ending places attribution in vijñāna-pariṇāma; it need not mean a physical location.
Asau resumes the relative clause; its initial a is elided after the preceding e.
Pariṇāma denotes change or transformation; its mechanism is developed in the next verse.
Sa refers back to transformation.
Ca connects the next statement.
Tridhā means in three ways, preparing the list in verse 2.

title: The three transformations
brief: Maturation, mentation, and presentation of an object are distinguished; the first is identified as all-seeded store consciousness.

words.note: Vipāka is the ripening of prior causal activity, not a moral judgment on each present event.
Manana names thinking or mentation; the compound says “known as manana.”
Ca coordinates the three transformations.
Vijñapti is rendered presentation here; representation and manifestation are interpretive alternatives.
Viṣayasya specifies what is presented: an object or field of experience.
Ca closes the list.
Tatra + ālaya + ākhyam identifies one item in the list. “Store” translates ālaya without making it a permanent container.
Vijñāna names discriminative awareness; the verse distinguishes its functions.
The store consciousness is identified with the maturation transformation.
Bīja, “seed,” is a causal metaphor for dispositions that can give rise to later experience.

title: Unnoticed appropriation and constant companions
brief: Two dense compounds describe store consciousness and its five constantly associated mental factors. Upādi is left open to closer philological review.

words.english: with unnoticed appropriation, location and presentation
words.note: The long compound compresses asaṃviditaka, upādi, sthāna and vijñaptika. This draft takes the appropriation and place as not consciously noticed; the internal scope is philologically unsettled.
words.alternative: whose appropriation and location are not distinctly known

words.note: Ca continues the description.
Tat refers to the store consciousness of verse 2.
Sadā qualifies the association with the following mental factors.

words.english: joined with contact, attention, feeling, recognition and volition
words.note: Sparśa, manaskāra, vit, saṃjñā and cetanā are five factors. Vit is taken here as feeling, consistent with vedanā in verse 4; anvitam means accompanied by.

title: Neutral feeling and a flowing stream
brief: The continuum is compared with a current; neither neutrality nor continuity establishes an unchanging self.

words.note: Upekṣā here specifies neutral feeling, rather than praising a cultivated meditative attainment.
Vedanā is the feeling tone of experience, not emotion in general.
Tatra + anivṛta + avyākṛtam: the store consciousness is not obscured by afflictions and is not classified as wholesome or unwholesome.
Ca links the characterization.
Tat points to the store consciousness.
Tathā extends the characterization to its associated factors.
Sparśa stands for the five factors named in verse 3.
Tac is tat before ca.
Ca connects the final description.
Vartate describes ongoing occurrence, not a fixed substance.
The comparison with a flow stresses causal continuity through change.

title: The turning away and mentation
brief: The first transformation ceases at arhatship; the account shifts to mind that both depends upon it and takes it as object.

words.note: Tasya refers back to the store consciousness; how its cessation is understood needs commentarial study.
Vyāvṛtti names a turning away or cessation. It is not the same word as parāvṛtti in verse 29.
The locative arhattve specifies the condition at which cessation occurs.
Tad is the object of āśritya: the preceding consciousness.
Āśritya is a dependent verbal form: “having relied on.”
Pravartate echoes the operation described in verse 1.
Tad-ālambam makes the same consciousness its cognitive support or object.
Manonāma gives the name manas, distinct here from the sixfold object awareness.
The second transformation is still called vijñāna.
Mananātmakam describes its activity, not a metaphysical self despite the word ātman inside the compound.

title: Four afflictions of mind
brief: The second transformation is obscured but ethically indeterminate and accompanied by four forms of self-fixation.

words.note: The instrumental plural marks what accompanies this mind.
Caturbhiḥ agrees with kleśaiḥ: four afflictions.
Sahitam means together with, describing association.
Nivṛta is the obscured reading printed here; avyākṛta means not assigned to wholesome or unwholesome classes. Contrast verse 4’s anivṛta.
Sadā marks their constant association with this afflicted mind.

words.english: called self-view, self-delusion, self-conceit and self-love
words.note: Four terms repeat ātma: dṛṣṭi, moha, māna and sneha. These designate afflictions, not the text’s endorsement of a self.

title: Where afflicted mind is absent
brief: The account specifies the shared sphere of associated factors and three conditions in which the second transformation is absent.

words.note: Yatrajaḥ compresses “born where”; the sphere must be understood from context.
Tanmayaiḥ describes the associated factors as having the corresponding character or sphere.
Anyaiḥ qualifies the further factors accompanying mind.
The instrumental forms continue the list of accompanying factors.
Ca + arhataḥ; the genitive identifies the person for whom this afflicted mind is absent.
Na negates its occurrence for an arhat.
Tat refers to the afflicted mentation, not to all awareness.
The second negation concerns the attainment of cessation.
Nirodha-samāpatti is a technical meditative attainment.
Mārge gives the setting for the third absence.
Lokottara qualifies the path as beyond ordinary worldly cognition.
The third negation concerns the supramundane path.
Ca joins the final exception.

title: Sixfold object awareness
brief: The second transformation concludes and the third begins: sixfold object apprehension classified in three ethical ways.

words.note: Dvitīya identifies the transformation just described in verses 5–7.
The same term pariṇāma links all three accounts.
Ayam resumes the preceding description; the apostrophe marks elision.
The third transformation is now introduced.
Ṣaḍvidhasya qualifies the object field as sixfold.
Yā introduces the apprehension identified by sā.
Viṣayasya + upalabdhiḥ joins the object and its apprehension in the written surface.
Sā resumes the feminine upalabdhiḥ.
Advayā here means neither of these two ethical classes, not the nonduality of subject and object discussed later.

title: Associated mental factors
brief: Sixfold apprehension is described by groups of mental factors and three kinds of feeling.

words.note: Sarvatraga means going everywhere: factors accompanying each instance in the relevant class.
Viniyata identifies factors whose occurrence depends on a particular object or circumstance.
Kuśala marks the wholesome class of mental factors.
Caitasa means belonging to mind; it should not be confused with a separate consciousness.
Asau refers to the sixfold apprehension of verse 8.
Saṃprayuktā expresses conjunction; the feminine form follows upalabdhiḥ.
Tathā extends the association to the remaining classes.
Kleśa names the primary afflictions listed in verses 11–12.
Upakleśa introduces the further afflictive factors enumerated next.
Trivedanā indicates three feeling tones, rather than three separate selves or minds.

title: Universal, specific and wholesome factors
brief: The list moves quickly between categories; “the first” refers back to verse 9, and the wholesome list continues into verse 11.

words.note: Ādyāḥ refers to the universal factors in the preceding verse.
Sparśādayaḥ recalls the five factors of verse 3; “are” is supplied for English.
Chanda, adhimokṣa and smṛti begin the object-specific list. These glosses are contextual, not dictionary quotations.
words.alternative: desire to act, determination and mindfulness

words.note: Saha coordinates the next pair.
Samādhi and dhī are joined in an instrumental dual, completing five object-specific factors.
Niyatāḥ closes the class begun with chanda.
Śraddhā + atha opens the wholesome factors; trust is not necessarily unexamined belief.
Hrī is reluctance to do what one oneself regards as wrong, distinct from the next term.
Apatrapā is moral reserve in relation to others; its contrast with hrī is a contextual study gloss.

title: Wholesome and primary afflictive factors
brief: The wholesome list finishes before kleśāḥ introduces afflictions; the first three wholesome roots are compressed as a triad.

words.note: Alobhādi abbreviates a list starting with alobha; the standard contextual expansion is non-greed, non-hatred and non-delusion.
Trayam signals three items; the preceding abbreviation is not just one factor.
Vīrya here is effort or energetic engagement.
Praśrabdhi describes ease or adaptability of body and mind, not mere passivity.
Sāpramādikā is read as sa-apramādikā, with non-negligence; the long ā matters.
Ahiṃsā explicitly negates harm. Contrast vihiṃsā in verse 13.
Kuśalāḥ closes the wholesome list; the verb is supplied in English.
Kleśāḥ begins the next class; the next verse continues it.
Rāga, pratigha and mūḍhi name the first three primary afflictions.

title: From primary to subsidiary afflictions
brief: Conceit, views and doubt complete the primary afflictions; anger and resentment begin the subsidiary list.

words.note: Māna, dṛś and vicikitsā complete the list begun in verse 11. “Views” is contextually afflictive here.
Ca closes the primary list.
The dual krodhopanahane names two factors. Lévi’s spelling is retained; modern editions may print krodhopanāhane.
Punaḥ marks a further group rather than repetition of the same factor.
Mrakṣa is taken as concealing or denying faults; the exact technical scope needs review.
Pradāśa is a harsh, contentious attitude, not a new act of physical violence.
Īrṣyā + atha joins the next item and a transition word.
Mātsarya concerns unwillingness to share or let others benefit.
Saha links the following item.
Māyā here names deceptive presentation; “illusion” alone would obscure its ethical function.

title: Further subsidiary afflictions
brief: This normalized transcription removes a misleading printed avagraha before vihiṃsā: harmfulness and shamelessness are two afflictions, not non-harming and shame.

words.note: Śāṭhya denotes crookedness or dissimulation in conduct.
Mada is self-intoxication or conceited elation, distinct from māna in verse 12.
Read vihiṃsā + ahrīḥ. The source transcription explicitly emends the print’s misleading avagraha; do not read avihiṃsā + hrīḥ.
Atrapā negates the concern named apatrapā in verse 10.
Styāna describes mental heaviness or inertia.
Lévi prints uddhavaḥ, retained here; the modern comparison has uddhataḥ. The draft gloss needs philological review.
Āśraddhya is the counterpart of śraddhā in verse 10.
Atha continues the list.
Kausīdya is reluctance to engage effort; the spelling is retained from this edition.
Pramāda is negligence, contrasting with apramāda in verse 11.
Muṣitā qualifies smṛtiḥ: recollection that has been lost or stolen away.
Together muṣitā smṛtiḥ names failure of recollection, not an additional wholesome factor.

title: Distraction and variable factors
brief: The final two pairs have a twofold status. The classification and technical English for vitarka/vicāra remain interpretive.

words.note: Vikṣepa is scattering of attention.
Asaṃprajanya starts with a negating a, elided after the preceding o.
Ca completes these subsidiary factors.
Kaukṛtya is concern over what was done or left undone; its ethical value can vary.
Middha is drowsiness or sleep, distinguished from the specific absence of cognition in verse 16.
Eva emphasizes the grouping.
Ca coordinates the list.
Vitarka is rendered as an initial directing or examination of thought; this is a debated technical term.
Ca joins the pair.
Vicāra is rendered as continuing examination; its relation to vitarka depends on the interpretive tradition.
Ca + iti closes the enumeration.
The wording groups the preceding material; the final pairs require the qualification that follows.
Dvaye points to regret/sleepiness and initial/sustained examination.
Dvidhā marks their variable ethical status; it does not mean four extra afflictions.

title: Sense consciousnesses as waves
brief: The five sensory consciousnesses arise according to conditions, singly or together, dependent upon root consciousness.

words.note: Pañcānām qualifies vijñānānām later in the verse; Sanskrit can separate agreeing words.
The locative mūlavijñāne identifies the supporting consciousness described earlier.
Yathāpratyayam makes occurrence conditional, not arbitrary.
Udbhava names the coming forth of the sensory consciousnesses.
The genitive plural belongs with “of the five.”
Saha allows simultaneous arising.
Na combines with vā to allow non-simultaneous occurrence.
Vā marks the alternative.
Taraṅgāṇām supplies the image for the arising of consciousnesses.
Yathā introduces the comparison, not a claim that consciousness is literally water.
Jale is locative: where waves arise.

title: When mental consciousness does not arise
brief: The exceptions concern non-cognitive states; the qualification acittaka must not be stretched to all sleep or all fainting.

words.note: Manovijñāna is mental cognition, distinguished from the five sensory consciousnesses of verse 15.

words.english: always, apart from the non-percipient state
words.note: Sarvadā + asaṃjñikāt compresses “always” and the first exception; the ablative goes with ṛte.
Ṛte governs the exceptions, whose endings mark exclusion.
The dual in samāpattidvaya refers contextually to the non-percipient and cessation attainments; the names are not spelled out here.
Middhāt appears as middhān before the following m through sound combination.
Mūrcchanāt is another state in the exclusion list.
Api continues the qualification.
Acittakāt limits the relevant states to those without active cognition; this draft does not generalize the exception to every sleep state.

title: Constructing and what is constructed
brief: The verse denies the constructed object as constructed. It should not be reduced without argument to a slogan denying every kind of reality.

words.note: This takes up pariṇāma from verse 1 after completing the threefold account.
Ayam identifies the transformation just described.
Vikalpa is discriminative construction; “imagination” alone can misleadingly suggest deliberate fantasy.
Yad introduces the object of construction.
The passive vikalpyate distinguishes what is constructed from the constructing activity.
Tena refers to vikalpa as the agent or means of construction.
Tan is tat before nāsti and resumes the constructed object.
Na + asti denies that object in the asserted mode; the scope is philosophically contested.
Tena + idam moves from the denial to the conclusion.
Sarvam scopes the conclusion across the field being discussed.
Vijñaptimātrakam has short a after ñ, unlike a typo in the modern digital comparison. “Only” is the force of mātra.

title: Seeds and reciprocal conditioning
brief: All-seeded consciousness undergoes transformations through reciprocal influence, producing particular constructions.

words.note: Sarvabījam recalls the store consciousness in verse 2.
Hi supports the causal explanation.
Vijñāna is the subject of yāti.
The printed pariṇāmas is retained; its syntax with yāti merits philological review rather than silent normalization.
The repeated tathā distributes over different transformations.
The repetition means various corresponding ways, not a redundant phrase to discard.
Yāti literally goes; here the draft takes it with transformation.
Anyonyavaśāt points to reciprocal dependence or control; the verse does not fully spell out every causal direction.
Yena links the transformation to the arising construction.
Vikalpa repeats the key term from verse 17.
Sa repeated with sa has a distributive force.
The second sa contributes “each particular,” rather than a second entity.
Jāyate describes coming into being under conditions.

title: Impressions and renewed maturation
brief: Impressions of action and of twofold grasping bring about a further maturation when the previous one is exhausted.

words.note: Karmaṇaḥ is genitive: whose impressions are involved.
Vāsanā names lasting conditioning or perfuming, not a consciously retained memory alone.
Grāhadvaya is interpreted as the grasper/grasped duality; this is a contextual reading, not two literal hands.
Saha marks the joint contribution of the two kinds of conditioning.
Kṣīṇe belongs with pūrvavipāke in a locative absolute: when the earlier maturation is spent.
Pūrva points to the preceding causal result.
Anyam qualifies the next maturation; initial a is elided after e.
Vipākam is the object of janayanti.
The plural verb fits the impressions as causal factors.
Tat connects the resulting maturation with the consciousness under discussion; the precise construction deserves review.

title: The imagined nature
brief: The imagined nature is whatever object is fashioned by a particular construction; its existence as thus imagined is denied.

words.note: The doubled yena distributes over any particular construction.
The repetition belongs with the first yena; this gloss renders its distributive force.
Vikalpena is instrumental, identifying the constructing activity.
Yad repeated picks out any object.
The second yad continues the distributive pattern.
Vastu is what is taken as an object or thing, without deciding its final ontological status.
The passive repeats the structure in verse 17.
Parikalpita names the first of the three natures, often rendered imagined or fabricated.
Eva + asau identifies the imagined object as this nature.
Svabhāva is a technical term here; “nature” must not silently imply an independent essence.
Na negates the following verb.
Sa refers to the imagined nature as such.
Vidyate means exists or is present; “is found” keeps the link to how the object is posited.

title: Dependent and perfected natures
brief: Construction arises dependently; the perfected is the dependent’s enduring absence of the previously described imagined nature.

words.note: Paratantra means dependent on another; its dependence is explained by conditions.
Tu marks the contrast with the imagined nature.
Vikalpa is here identified under its dependent aspect.
Pratyayodbhava specifies causal dependence; it is not an unconditioned absolute.
Niṣpanna abbreviates the perfected or fully accomplished nature.
Tasya refers to the dependent nature. The genitive is rendered “in that” to express the dependent nature’s absence of the imagined, not the absence of the dependent itself.
Pūrveṇa points to the imagined nature of verse 20, with rahitatā indicating absence of it.
Sadā qualifies the absence rather than a temporal event of destroying something real.
Rahitatā means being devoid of; it does not say that all dependent functioning disappears.
Tu distinguishes the final characterization.
Yā relates the absence to the perfected nature.

title: Neither different nor identical
brief: The perfected and dependent are not separate things or simply identical. The final pronoun relation is a study interpretation pending specialist review.

words.note: Ataḥ draws an inference from the relation in verse 21.
Eva emphasizes this inference.
Sa is taken as the perfected nature.
Na + eva + anyaḥ rejects complete difference.
Na + ananyaḥ rejects uncomplicated identity as well.
Paratantrataḥ uses an ablative expression to name what it is compared with.
The analogy suggests a property and what has that property, without establishing a separate substance.
Vācya marks the prescribed formulation.
Na + adṛṣṭe belongs to a locative absolute: while this has not been seen.
Asmin is read as the perfected nature; this identification is interpretive.
Sa is read as the dependent nature in the concluding clause.
Dṛśyate is passive: becomes seen or discerned.

title: Three kinds of absence of own-nature
brief: The teaching that all phenomena lack own-nature is made with three distinct senses in view.

words.note: Trividhasya qualifies the set of natures, not three unrelated substances.
Svabhāvasya is the genitive corresponding to the three natures just explained.
Trividhām qualifies absence of own-nature.
Niḥsvabhāvatā negates independent or intrinsic nature; its sense must be distinguished for each case.
Sandhāya means having in view or intending, explaining why one teaching has multiple senses.
Sarvadharmāṇām gives the scope of the teaching.
Deśitā is a past passive participle; the teacher is not named in this verse.
The repeated term states the general teaching whose differentiated intention is being explained.

title: Character and independent arising
brief: The first nature lacks own-nature by its supposed character; the next does not arise through itself. The compact wording should not erase this distinction.

words.note: Prathama refers to the imagined nature.
Lakṣaṇena + eva explains the sense in which the first lacks own-nature.
Niḥsvabhāva predicates the absence, rather than naming another hidden essence.
Apara refers to the dependent nature, the second in the series.
Punaḥ marks a new sense of the teaching.
Na denies independent arising.
Svayaṃbhāva is being or arising by itself; the dependent depends on conditions.
Etasya + iti marks the reasoning about the second nature; the compressed syntax remains interpretive.
Aparā distinguishes this absence from the first kind.
The same phrase must be read with the distinct reason just given.

title: Suchness and representation only
brief: The ultimate meaning and suchness are linked with representation-only; “always so” describes suchness, not an eternal individual consciousness.

words.note: Dharmāṇām qualifies the ultimate or highest sense.
Paramārtha may mean ultimate reality or highest meaning; the draft does not settle the whole doctrinal debate.
Ca continues the account of absence of own-nature.
Sa points back to the nature under discussion.
Yataḥ introduces its identification as suchness.
Tathatā + api names being just so, rather than a new object added to experience.
Saḥ resumes the same referent.
Sarvakālam qualifies being thus.
Tathābhāvāt is ablative and supplies the reason for the name tathatā.
Sā + eva emphasizes the identification.
Vijñaptimātratā is the abstract noun corresponding to vijñaptimātra in verse 17.

title: The persistence of twofold grasping
brief: The verse turns to practice: merely discussing representation-only does not remove the latent tendency to subject/object grasping.

words.note: Yāvat pairs with tāvat to frame the condition and its continuing consequence.
The locative ending names what consciousness has yet to become established in.
Vijñānam is the subject; the printed wording is retained.
Lévi prints nāvatiṣṭhati, retained here. A familiar modern reading is nāvatiṣṭhate; this draft does not silently substitute it.

words.english: the latent tendency of twofold grasping
words.note: Grāhadvayasya + anuśaya names the underlying tendency toward grasper and grasped, not only an explicit belief.
Tāvat closes the temporal correlation begun by yāvat.
Na negates the cessation of the tendency.
Vinivartate means turns back or comes to an end.

title: The trap of making it an object
brief: Holding up “representation only” as something graspable fails the very condition of establishment in it.

words.note: Vijñaptimātram is the content of a thought being examined here.
Eva + idam completes the quoted claim, “this is just representation.”
Iti closes the quotation; it is not an extra object in the claim.
Api shows that even this apparently correct formulation can remain reifying.
Hi introduces the reason.
Upalambhataḥ identifies the problem as taking hold of something, not the bare use of words.
Sthāpayan is a present participle: while placing or setting something before oneself.
Agrataḥ literally means in front; here it describes objectification.
Kiṃcit leaves the object unspecified, including representation-only itself.
Tanmātre refers to representation-only without installing a separate grasped object.
Nāvatiṣṭhate denies successful establishment in the condition just asserted.

title: No grasped object, no grasping
brief: Retain Lévi’s distinct wording: yadālambanaṃ vijñānaṃ and vijñānamātratve. It is not silently harmonized with the modern vijñaptimātratve reading.

words.note: Yadā + ālambanam. Lévi has this joined wording, without the modern inserted tu and with vijñānam in the next word.
Vijñānam is retained from Lévi; some modern texts read jñānam here.
Na + eva + upalabhate negates taking hold of an object-support.
Tadā pairs with yadā at the start.
Sthitam states the resulting condition; it is not an instruction to manufacture a new object.
Lévi prints vijñānamātratve here; this differs from the familiar vijñaptimātratve. The distinction remains visible in the English.

words.english: in the absence of the grasped
words.note: Grāhya-abhāve is a locative expression; the scan supports grāhyābhāve, not the duplicated bhā in the digital comparison.
Tad-agrahāt states the reason. This draft reads the absence of grasping in correlation with the absence of a grasped object; pronoun scope needs review.

title: Supramundane knowledge and transformation of basis
brief: Non-apprehension is associated with supramundane knowledge and transformation of the basis through abandoning a twofold burden.

words.note: Acitta is a technical negation, not necessarily unconscious stupor. Its relation to the following knowledge requires care.
Anupalambha retains bh as visible in the scan; the digital comparison’s missing consonant is not followed.
Asau points to the condition described in verse 28.
Jñāna appears here, distinct in wording from vijñāna in the previous verse.
Lokottara characterizes the knowledge as beyond ordinary worldly cognition.
Ca coordinates the characterization.
Tat resumes the knowledge or condition just described.
Āśrayasya is genitive: the basis whose transformation is described.
Parāvṛtti names a turning about of the basis; it should not be conflated with an eternal substrate.
Dvidhā qualifies the removal; the verse itself does not list both categories.
Dauṣṭhulya-hāni is removal of the encumbering or unfit condition. Identification with particular two-obstruction schemes is commentarial, not spelled out here.

title: The unobstructed element
brief: The closing names are presented as the text’s claims; the draft does not turn them into an independent doctrinal verdict.

words.note: Sa resumes the transformed condition or basis.
Eva + anāsrava describes freedom from the afflictive outflows; “pure” alone would hide the technical term.
Dhātu can mean element or domain; it need not be read as a material substance.
Acintya denies that ordinary conceptual thought encompasses it.
Kuśala returns from the earlier ethical lists in this final description.
Dhruva suggests stability; how this relates to impermanence is a doctrinal question, not resolved by this gloss.
Sukha here is ease or well-being, not ordinary sensory gratification alone.
Vimukti-kāya uses body in the sense of an achieved embodiment or collection, not necessarily a physical body.
Asau resumes the condition being named.
Dharmākhya supplies the name Dharma; in context it can be read with kāya, “Dharma body.”
Ayam points to the same body or condition.
Mahāmuneḥ is genitive, attributing this to the great sage, traditionally the Buddha.
